An image built on the server ([caddysecurebuild](#caddysecurebuild-ingress)) is rebuilt with `--pull` instead, on the newest base images. `--recreate` recreates every shared app's containers (`--force-recreate`) even when nothing changed; their data is kept, but apps using them lose them while they restart. Both need `--apply`. Mind major versions: Postgres does not start on the data of an older major version.

When a shared app loses a link (say its `monitoring` is removed), the deploy with `--apply` removes the link and recreates the shared app without it.

Shared apps removed from the config are reported as `orphaned` and keep running; stop them with `docker compose -p compost-<kind>-<name> down`.

## Shared app types

A server has at most one ingress, and any number of databases (Postgres, MariaDB, MySQL), key-value stores (Valkey, Redis), storage (Garage, external S3), OIDC providers, monitoring apps, workflow servers (Temporal) and communication apps (channels for notifications: webhook, Slack, Mattermost, Discord, Matrix, email; see [Notifications](Notifications.md)). Every shared app has a `name` (lowercase letters, digits and `-`, up to 31 characters, starting with a letter), a `type`, a `version` and optionally an `image`. Type-specific settings go in `configuration`.

### caddy (`ingress`)

Reverse proxy for every app's domains, with automatic HTTPS.

```yaml
shared:
  ingress:
    - name: caddy-main
      type: caddy
      version: 2
      configuration:
        http_port: 80
        https_port: 443
        tls: auto
        acme_email: admin@example.com
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `2` | Only `2` |
| `image` | `caddy:<version>-alpine` | |
| `configuration.http_port` | `80` | Host port |
| `configuration.https_port` | `443` | Host port, TCP and UDP |
| `configuration.tls` | `auto` | How sites get certificates: `auto`, `internal` or `off`, see [TLS](#tls) |
| `configuration.acme_email` | – | Contact for the ACME account. Only with `tls: auto` |
| `configuration.networks` | `[]` | Existing Docker networks Caddy joins too, so `sites` can reach containers compost doesn't manage. Never created: `server deploy` fails if one is missing |
| `configuration.sites[]` | `[]` | Sites written by hand: `name`, `domains`, and `config`, the inside of a Caddyfile site block |
| `configuration.access_log` | `false` | Log every request, as JSON, to Caddy's output. With [`monitoring`](#monitoring-shared-apps), the log goes to OpenObserve. An app's site gets it on the app's next `app deploy` |

```yaml
      configuration:
        networks: [shop_default]
        sites:
          - name: shop
            domains: [shop.example.com]
            config: |
              reverse_proxy backend:5000
```

`sites` are for services compost doesn't deploy, typically while [migrating](Migration.md). A domain belongs to a site or to an app, not both: `app deploy` refuses a domain a site serves, and `server deploy` refuses a site for a domain an app serves.

#### TLS

`configuration.tls` applies to every domain Caddy serves, apps' and `sites` alike:

| Value | Certificates | Ports |
|---|---|---|
| `auto` | From Let's Encrypt, renewed by Caddy. Every domain needs public DNS pointing to the server and port 80 or 443 reachable from the internet before the first deploy. HTTP redirects to HTTPS | `http_port` and `https_port` |
| `internal` | Signed by Caddy's own local CA. Browsers warn unless they trust its root certificate, `data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt` in the Caddy folder. For test servers and domains without public DNS | `http_port` and `https_port` |
| `off` | None: sites are served over plain HTTP. For a local machine, or behind another proxy that terminates TLS | `http_port` only; `https_port` is not published |

`acme_email` is the contact Let's Encrypt uses for expiry warnings; compost refuses the config when it is set with any `tls` other than `auto`. Certificates are kept in `data/` (see [Files and folders](Files-and-Folders.md)) and are part of `server backup`, so a restored server doesn't request them again.

With [`monitoring`](#monitoring-shared-apps), Caddy also serves its Prometheus metrics (requests, durations, sizes per host) on port 9180 inside its container, not published on the host, and the collector scrapes them. This needs Caddy 2.8 or newer; the default image is.

Caddy runs as the server user, so its files can be backed up and removed without root. Hosts and paths no app uses get a 404. When an app is deployed, Caddy is reloaded, not restarted; a site that fails `caddy validate` is rolled back and fails the deploy.

### caddysecurebuild (`ingress`)

Caddy as above, built on the server with request filtering, next to a [CrowdSec](https://www.crowdsec.net/) agent:

- **Bans.** The agent reads Caddy's access log and bans addresses that attack, e.g. a burst of more than 5 POST requests answered 401 or 403 (brute-force logins; one is forgotten every 10 seconds), path traversal, SQL injection probes or scans for admin pages. It also gets CrowdSec's community blocklist. A banned address gets 403 on every site that enforces bans, for `ban_duration`.
- **AppSec.** Caddy sends every request to CrowdSec's AppSec component first, which blocks known exploits (CrowdSec's virtual patching and generic rules) with 403. Optionally, it also checks the OWASP Core Rule Set, out of band: a match doesn't block the request, but repeated matches ban the address.
- **Rate limits.** Zones you define: at most `events` matching requests per address within `window`; more get 429.

All keys of [caddy](#caddy-ingress) apply, plus `security`. Everything in it is optional:

```yaml
shared:
  ingress:
    - name: caddy-main
      type: caddysecurebuild
      version: 2
      configuration:
        tls: auto
        acme_email: admin@example.com
        security:
          crowdsec:
            whitelist: [203.0.113.0/24]   # never banned: your office, monitoring
            ban_duration: 4h
          appsec:
            crs: false
          defaults:                       # what a site gets unless its own `security` says otherwise
            bans: true
            appsec: true
            rate_limits: [login]          # default: every zone below
          rate_limits:
            - name: login
              paths: [/login, /wp-login.php, /user/login]
              methods: [POST]
              events: 10
              window: 1m
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `2` | Major version of the `caddy:<version>-builder` and `caddy:<version>-alpine` images the build uses |
| `image` | – | Not accepted: the image is built |
| `security.crowdsec.whitelist` | `[]` | IP addresses and networks (`203.0.113.0/24`) that are never banned. CrowdSec never bans private addresses either (`10.0.0.0/8`, `192.168.0.0/16`, …) |
| `security.crowdsec.ban_duration` | `4h` | How long a ban lasts, e.g. `30m`, `1h30m` |
| `security.crowdsec.collections` | `[]` | Hub collections installed besides `crowdsecurity/caddy`, `crowdsecurity/base-http-scenarios`, `crowdsecurity/appsec-virtual-patching` and `crowdsecurity/appsec-generic-rules`, e.g. `crowdsecurity/wordpress` |
| `security.crowdsec.scenarios` | `[]` | Hub scenarios installed besides those of the collections |
| `security.appsec.crs` | `false` | Also check the OWASP Core Rule Set (`crowdsecurity/appsec-crs`), out of band |
| `security.defaults.bans` | `true` | Sites enforce bans |
| `security.defaults.appsec` | `true` | Sites check requests with AppSec |
| `security.defaults.rate_limits` | all zones | Zones sites use, by name |
| `security.rate_limits[].name` | required | Zone name |
| `security.rate_limits[].paths` | every path | Request paths; `*` matches anything, e.g. `/api/*` |
| `security.rate_limits[].methods` | every method | e.g. `[POST]` |
| `security.rate_limits[].events` | required | Requests allowed per address in `window` |
| `security.rate_limits[].window` | required | e.g. `10s`, `1m` |
| `sites[].security` | – | A site's own choice, like an app's (see [Ingress links](Applications.md#ingress-links)) |

Apps choose per ingress entry with [`security`](Applications.md#request-filtering); an entry without it gets `defaults`. A site's zones count each address separately for each site. CrowdSec reads the log of every site, including sites with `bans: false`, so an address banned for attacking one site is blocked on all sites that enforce bans.

Changing `defaults` or a zone applies to every site on the next `server deploy`, with a reload. When you switch an existing `caddy` to this type, apps' sites get the defaults right away, but they share their rate-limit counters until each app's next `app deploy`. `server deploy` refuses to remove a zone that a deployed app's `security` names, and switching back to `type: caddy` while an app has `security`: deploy those apps without it first.

**The build.** The first `server deploy --apply` builds the image on the server (`build/Dockerfile` in the Caddy folder), which takes a few minutes and needs internet access. The image is tagged `compost-caddysecurebuild-<name>:<hash of the Dockerfile>`, so later deploys reuse it until compost pins newer modules. `--pull` rebuilds it on the newest Caddy images.

**The agent** is the container `compost-ingress-<name>-crowdsec` (image `crowdsecurity/crowdsec`). It's only on a network it shares with Caddy, so apps and other shared apps can't reach it. Its state (bans, its registration with CrowdSec) is in the Docker volumes `compost-ingress-<name>_crowdsec-data` and `_crowdsec-config`; it is not part of `server backup`. If the agent is down or still starting, requests pass unchecked rather than failing.

To see and lift bans:

```sh
docker exec compost-ingress-caddy-main-crowdsec cscli decisions list
docker exec compost-ingress-caddy-main-crowdsec cscli alerts list
docker exec compost-ingress-caddy-main-crowdsec cscli decisions delete --ip 198.51.100.7
```

Lock yourself out of a site and it's usually a ban: lift it, then add your address to `whitelist`. Behind another proxy or a CDN, every request comes from the proxy's address; this type is for servers that face the internet directly.

### postgres (`database`)

A Postgres server. Each app link gets its own database and user.

```yaml
shared:
  database:
    - name: postgres18
      type: postgres
      version: 18
      image: postgres:18-alpine
      configuration:
        root_password: …    # in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | required | Major version, matched against apps' `version` requirements |
| `image` | `postgres:<version>` | An official `postgres` image or a compatible one |
| `configuration.root_password` | generated | Superuser password. Secret. Can't change after the first deploy |

Postgres is not published on a host port. Only containers on its network `compost-db-<name>` reach it, at host name `<name>`, port 5432.

### mariadb and mysql (`database`)

A MariaDB or MySQL server. They work alike: each app link gets its own database (`utf8mb4`) and a user with all rights on it, and nothing else.

```yaml
shared:
  database:
    - name: mariadb11
      type: mariadb             # or mysql
      version: 11               # mysql: 8
      configuration:
        root_password: …        # in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `11` (mariadb), `8` (mysql) | Major version, matched against apps' `version` requirements |
| `image` | `mariadb:<version>`, `mysql:<version>` | An official image or a compatible one |
| `configuration.root_password` | generated | Password of `root`. Secret, without quotes or `\`. Can't change after the first deploy |

Like Postgres, it is reached only on `compost-db-<name>`, at host name `<name>`, port 3306. User names are at most 32 characters (MySQL's limit, kept for MariaDB too, so databases can move between them): a longer default name is cut and ends in a short hash, e.g. `shop_production_custo_5f6407f3`; `app state` shows it.

Backups use `mariadb-dump` / `mysqldump` with `--single-transaction`, so InnoDB tables are copied consistently without stopping the app. App dumps leave out `DEFINER` clauses, so they load into a copy with another user. A server backup holds every database, user and grant, and restores onto the same major version.

### valkey and redis (`keyvalue`)

A key-value store that apps link to (see [Key-value links](Applications.md#key-value-links)). Valkey is the open-source (BSD) fork of Redis; Redis 8 is licensed AGPLv3 or RSAL/SSPL.

```yaml
shared:
  keyvalue:
    - name: valkey
      type: valkey             # or redis
      version: 9               # redis: 8
      configuration:
        max_memory: 512mb
        eviction: allkeys-lru  # for a cache
        password: …            # in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `9` (valkey), `8` (redis) | Major version. Valkey needs 9.1 or newer (the `9` image is): it locks each app's user to its own database |
| `image` | `valkey/valkey:<version>`, `redis:<version>` | |
| `configuration.password` | generated | Password of the `default` user, for compost and you. Secret; a new value replaces the old one with the next deploy |
| `configuration.max_memory` | none | e.g. `512mb`: above it the server evicts keys by `eviction` |
| `configuration.eviction` | `noeviction` | `allkeys-lru`, `allkeys-lfu`, `allkeys-random`, `volatile-lru`, `volatile-lfu`, `volatile-random` or `volatile-ttl` |

It is reached only on `compost-kv-<name>`, at host name `<name>`, port 6379, and keeps its data with AOF (every write is logged) in `data/`. Each link's user is in the server's ACL file, which compost writes from the link records (passwords only as hashes) and loads with `ACL LOAD`, so linking an app never restarts it; a change of `password`, `max_memory` or `eviction` does.

A server backup takes a fresh snapshot (`dump.rdb`) of all databases; `server restore` loads it and then turns AOF on again.

### garage and s3 (`storage`)

S3-compatible object storage that apps link to (see [Storage links](Applications.md#storage-links)).

**garage**: compost runs [Garage](https://garagehq.deuxfleurs.fr), a small S3 server (AGPL), as a single node. Each link gets its own bucket and key.

```yaml
shared:
  storage:
    - name: storage
      type: garage
      version: 2
      configuration:
        url: https://files.example.com   # optional: the S3 API on this domain, through the ingress
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `2` | Major version; compost pins the image (`dxflrs/garage:v2.3.0`) |
| `image` | – | Another image |
| `configuration.url` | – | Public URL of the S3 API, served by the ingress; apps get it as `s3_public_endpoint` |
| `configuration.region` | `garage` | Region name clients sign requests with |
| `configuration.capacity` | `100G` | The node's weight in Garage's layout; not a quota |

It runs as the server user, keeps its metadata and objects in `meta/` and `data/`, and is reached on `compost-storage-<name>` at `http://<name>:3900`. The first link applies a one-node layout. Garage covers what apps usually need (buckets, multipart uploads, presigned URLs) but not everything AWS has: no versioning, object lock or bucket policies. A server backup stops Garage briefly and copies its folders.

A Garage on one server can also be the [S3 backup target](Backup-and-Restore.md#s3-targets) of another: create a bucket and key for it with `docker exec compost-storage-<name> /garage …` and use its `url` as `endpoint`.

**s3**: an S3 service compost doesn't run. It needs only `external`; links pin it with `instance` and give their bucket and key.

```yaml
shared:
  storage:
    - name: aws
      type: s3
      external:
        endpoint: https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
        region: eu-central-1
        network: minio_default       # optional: a Docker network to reach it on
```

`server state` shows it as `not checked`: only the links have credentials.

MinIO is not a built-in type: its community edition is distributed as source only since October 2025 and its repository was archived in April 2026. An existing MinIO works as `s3`. RustFS and SeaweedFS may become types later.

### keycloak (`oidc`)

An OpenID Connect provider for app logins. It needs a `postgres` database with version 18 or newer and the ingress, both on the same server: compost creates its database `compost_oidc_<name>_db` and routes the domain of `url` to it.

```yaml
shared:
  oidc:
    - name: keycloak
      type: keycloak
      version: 26
      configuration:
        url: https://auth.example.com
        admin_password: …   # in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `26` | Major version |
| `image` | `quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.6` for 26 | Required for other versions |
| `configuration.url` | required | Public URL, `https://<domain>` or `http://<domain>[:port]`, no path |
| `configuration.admin_user` | `admin` | Administrator in realm `master` |
| `configuration.admin_password` | generated | Secret. Only used on the first start; can't change later |
| `configuration.database.instance` | – | The database to use, when several match |

Its data lives in that database: back them up and restore them together. Apps reach it on network `compost-oidc-<name>` at `http://<name>:8080`. Keycloak gets 180 s to start. See [Applications](Applications.md#oidc-links) for linking apps to it.

### openobserve (`monitoring`)

Collects logs, metrics and traces of apps and shared apps, and shows them in [OpenObserve](https://openobserve.ai)'s UI. It runs two containers:
- **openobserve** stores the data in `shared/monitoring/<name>/data/` and serves the UI. Only the collector and the ingress reach it.
- **collector**, an [OpenTelemetry Collector](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/), receives what apps send and forwards it to OpenObserve. Apps reach it on network `compost-monitoring-<name>` at host name `<name>`, without credentials; only the collector knows OpenObserve's password.

```yaml
shared:
  monitoring:
    - name: monitoring
      type: openobserve
      version: 1
      configuration:
        url: https://logs.example.com
        retention_days: 30
        root_password: …    # in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `1` | Major version |
| `image` | `openobserve/openobserve:vX.Y.Z` for 1 | Required for other versions |
| `configuration.url` | – | Public URL of the UI, `https://<domain>` or `http://<domain>[:port]`, no path. compost routes its domain through the ingress. Without it, the UI is not reachable |
| `configuration.root_email` | `admin@compost.local` | Login of the root user. Can't change after the first deploy |
| `configuration.root_password` | generated | Secret. 8 or more characters with a lowercase and an uppercase letter, a digit and a special character, as OpenObserve requires. Can't change after the first deploy |
| `configuration.retention_days` | OpenObserve's (10 years) | Days data is kept |
| `configuration.forward_port` | `24224` | Port on the server's `127.0.0.1` where Docker delivers the output of linked containers. Each monitoring app needs its own |
| `configuration.container_metrics` | `true` | CPU, memory, network and disk I/O of every container on the server. The collector reads them from the Docker socket, mounted read-only; that gives the collector control over Docker, like root on the server. `false` leaves the socket out |
| `configuration.collector_image` | `otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:X.Y.Z` | |

What ends up in OpenObserve (organization `default`):
- **Logs** stream `docker`: the output of linked containers, with `fluent_tag` (`<instance>.<service>`: the compose service, e.g. `myapp-prod.backend`; for a shared app its plain name, e.g. `compost-ingress-caddy-main.caddy`), `container_name`, `source` (`stdout`/`stderr`) and the Compose project and service. A line that is a JSON object, like Caddy's log, is stored as fields: `body_level`, `body_msg`, `body_request_method`, `body_status` and so on, nested objects below the third level as JSON text (e.g. `body_request_headers`). Other lines stay in `body`.
- **Logs** stream `default`, **traces** and **metrics** that apps send with OpenTelemetry (OTLP).
- **Metrics** scraped from the Prometheus endpoints of links, labeled `compost_app`, `compost_prefix` and `compost_service` (named like in `fluent_tag`), and the `container_*` metrics.

Log in with `root_email` and `root_password`; compost writes both to `connectors/monitoring/<name>/root-connector.yaml` on the server. Apps link to it with [`services.monitoring`](Applications.md#monitoring-links).

The log driver sends asynchronously: linked containers start and run while the collector is down, and `docker logs` keeps working.

### temporal (`workflow`)

A [Temporal](https://temporal.io) server for durable workflows, which apps link to (see [Workflow links](Applications.md#workflow-links)). It needs a `postgres` database with version 13 or newer on the same server: compost creates two databases on it, `compost_workflow_<name>_db` and `compost_workflow_<name>_visibility`. With `ui`, it also serves Temporal's web UI on a domain through the ingress, with a login through an OIDC provider.

```yaml
shared:
  workflow:
    - name: temporal
      type: temporal
      version: 1
      configuration:
        ui:
          url: https://temporal.example.com
          oidc: {realm: staff}       # users log in from this keycloak realm
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `1` | Major version; compost pins the images (`temporalio/server:vX.Y.Z`) |
| `image` | – | Another server image |
| `configuration.admin_tools_image` | `temporalio/admin-tools` with the tag of the server image | Sets up the database schema and runs the `temporal` CLI for compost. Needed when `image` has no tag |
| `configuration.history_shards` | `4` | Temporal's shard count. Can't change after the first deploy |
| `configuration.database.instance` | – | The database to use, when several match |
| `configuration.dynamic_config` | – | Temporal's [dynamic config](https://docs.temporal.io/references/dynamic-configuration), e.g. `{limit.maxIDLength: [{value: 255}]}`. A change is applied without a restart |
| `configuration.ui.url` | – | Public URL of the web UI, `https://<domain>` or `http://<domain>[:port]`, no path. Without `ui`, there is no UI |
| `configuration.ui.oidc` | – | Log in to the UI through an OIDC provider: `type` (default `keycloak`), `instance` (when several match), `realm` (default `compost-workflow-<name>`) |
| `configuration.ui.anonymous` | `false` | `true` serves the UI without a login, instead of `oidc`. Anyone who reaches it can start, signal and terminate every workflow |
| `configuration.ui.image` | `temporalio/ui:X.Y.Z` | |

The project runs four containers:
- **schema** creates or updates Temporal's tables, then exits. It runs before the server on every start, and does nothing when the tables are current.
- **server**, reached by apps on network `compost-wf-<name>` at `<name>:7233`. Its Prometheus metrics are on port 9090, not published.
- **admin**, Temporal's admin tools, where compost runs the `temporal` CLI to create and delete namespaces. `docker exec compost-workflow-<name>-admin temporal …` gives you the same CLI.
- **ui**, with `ui`.

With `oidc`, the link creates a client in the realm; the realm's users can log in to the UI and see every namespace. compost creates no users: add them in Keycloak's admin console, or name the realm of your staff with `realm`. Temporal's own API has no login: an app on `compost-wf-<name>` can reach every namespace, not only its own.

Upgrade Temporal one minor version at a time (e.g. `1.31` to `1.32`), as Temporal requires: set `image` (and `admin_tools_image`, if `image` has no tag) to each version in turn and deploy. The schema container brings the tables up to date before the new server starts.

Workflows and namespaces live in the two databases and are saved with them; a server backup adds the shard count. `server restore` starts Temporal after its databases are loaded.

## Monitoring shared apps

`monitoring` on a shared app sends its output, and the metrics it serves, to a monitoring app:

```yaml
shared:
  ingress:
    - name: caddy-main
      type: caddy
      configuration:
        access_log: true
      monitoring: {}
  database:
    - name: postgres18
      type: postgres
      version: 18
      monitoring: {metrics: false}
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `monitoring.instance` | – | The monitoring app to use, when there are several |
| `monitoring.logs` | `true` | Collect the output of its containers |
| `monitoring.metrics` | `true` | Scrape its metrics, if it serves any: Caddy and Temporal do |

Caddy, Postgres, Keycloak and Temporal can be monitored. External shared apps and monitoring apps can't. It works in both directions: OpenObserve's domain is served by the Caddy that sends its logs to it. On the first deploy, Caddy starts before OpenObserve, and Docker keeps Caddy's output in a small buffer and sends it once the collector runs.

## External databases

A database compost doesn't run (an existing Postgres, MariaDB or MySQL container, or a hosted one such as AWS RDS) can be added with `external`. Apps then link to it like to any database, and `app backup` dumps it.

```yaml
shared:
  database:
    - name: shop-db                    # an existing container on this server
      type: postgres
      version: 16                      # its major version
      external:
        host: db                       # service or container name
        network: shop_default          # existing network to reach it on
    - name: rds-main                   # AWS RDS
      type: postgres
      version: 16
      external:
        host: main.abc123.eu-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com
        sslmode: require
      configuration:                   # optional; root_password in the secrets file
        root_user: postgres
        root_password: …
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `external.host` | required | Host name or address, as the app's containers see it |
| `external.port` | `5432`, `3306` | |
| `external.network` | – | Existing Docker network the database is on; linked services join it. Without it, containers reach the host like any other address |
| `external.sslmode` | – | `disable`, `allow`, `prefer`, `require`, `verify-ca` or `verify-full`; used by compost's own clients, and added to `db_url` for Postgres (MySQL drivers each name it differently: set it in the app) |
| `external.allow_purge` | `false` | Let `--purge database` drop databases there (needs root credentials) |
| `configuration.root_user` | `postgres`, `root` | Superuser, if compost may create databases there |
| `configuration.root_password` | – | Its password; secret. A new value replaces the stored one; a deploy without it keeps the stored credentials |

What compost does with it:
- **Runs nothing.** `server deploy` only checks that `network` exists and stores how to reach it. `server state` checks that it answers (`external, accepting connections`); if it doesn't, the state is `DEGRADED`.
- **Links pin it.** A link uses an external database only with `instance: <name>`, so adding one never changes which database other apps get.
- **Without root credentials**, links name an existing database, user and password (`db_name`, `db_user`, `db_password`), and compost creates nothing. **With them**, compost creates databases and users as on its own Postgres.
- **Backups** run `pg_dump` and `psql` (or the MariaDB/MySQL tools) in a temporary container of the type's image on the server. The credentials go into a file readable only by the server user, deleted after the run, never onto a command line. `server backup` leaves external databases out: `app backup` saves the apps' databases.
- **Never destroys data by accident.** `--purge database` keeps databases there, with a warning, unless root credentials are set and `allow_purge: true`.
- Removed from `compost-server.yaml` while no app links to it, it is forgotten by the next `server deploy`.

Database names and users must be lowercase letters, digits and `_` (as compost's own); rename others before linking.

## Inspecting links

```sh
compost connector list
```

```
database
└─ postgres18  postgres 18  running
   ├─ myapp-prod/main-db  database myapp_prod_main_db, user myapp_prod_main_db  app: deployed
   └─ myapp-staging/main-db  database myapp_staging_main_db, user myapp_staging_main_db  app: deployed
ingress
└─ caddy-main  caddy 2  running
   ├─ myapp-prod/site  example.com  / → myapp-prod-web:8080  app: deployed
   └─ myapp-staging/site  staging.example.com  / → myapp-staging-web:8080  app: deployed
```

Links of shared apps (Keycloak's database and domain, Temporal's databases, domain and login) show as `shared <kind>/<name>/<entry>`. A link whose instance no longer exists shows as a leftover record.

## Disk space

Pulls and builds leave old images and build cache behind. `server prune` shows how the server's disk is used, then removes what no container needs:

```sh
compost server prune --dry-run     # disk usage and what would be removed
compost server prune [--yes]
```

```
Disk /: 41.2 GB free of 80.0 GB (49% used)
Docker:
  Images            16.0GB  reclaimable 12.5GB (78%)
  Build Cache       10.2GB  reclaimable 5.4GB
compost: backups folder 3.2 GB, releases 410.0 MB (sources; their images are in Docker's)

Unused images to remove:
  myorg/web:1.4                         210MB
  compost-caddysecurebuild-caddy-main:9f2c…  95MB
Also removed: dangling images (<none>) and the build cache.
Kept: 12 release images for `app rollback` (`deployment.releases` sets how many).
```

It removes every tagged image that no container uses, running or stopped, including images of other software on the server; the dangling images; and all of the build cache, so the next `build: true` deploy builds from scratch. The images kept for [rollback](Applications.md#releases-and-rollback) (`compost-release/…`) stay: an image that is also a release image only loses its other name. Volumes and containers are never touched, and neither are backups: [`backup prune`](Backup-and-Restore.md#deleting-old-archives) deletes old archives. It asks before removing anything unless `--yes`, and holds the server's lock, so it never removes an image that a running deploy has pulled but not started yet.

## Locks

Commands that change a server hold a lock (`~/.compost-server/lock/`), so two can't run at once. If a command was killed and left it behind, the next one prints who held it; add `--force-unlock` to remove it.

---

<!-- Secrets.md -->

# Secrets

Passwords and other per-instance values (domains, database credentials, OIDC users) live in **overlays**: YAML files merged over `compost.yaml`. Store an overlay on the server with `app deploy --secret` (or `secret deploy`), so every machine and CI deploys the instance with `compost.yaml` alone. For an instance on your machine you can also keep it local and pass it with `-f`.

## Rules

- Commit only examples: `.compost.secrets.example.yaml`, `.compost-staging.example.yaml`. compost never loads `*.example.yaml` by itself.
- Keep the real files out of Git, e.g. with `.compost-*.yaml` and `.compost.*.yaml` in `.gitignore`, keeping the examples with `!*.example.yaml`.
- Files named `.compost-*.yaml` or `.compost.*.yaml`, and every file passed with `-f`, are never uploaded with the sources.
- Passwords you leave out are generated on the first deploy (32 hexadecimal characters; OpenObserve's root password starts with `Compost-` to meet its rules), stored on the server and reused by later deploys.
- On the server, secret files have mode `0600`. Secrets never appear in output, stored configs or remote command lines. `--dry-run` names files with secrets but never shows them, also with `--diff`, and shows variable names, not values.

## Overlays stored on the server

```sh
compost app deploy --dry-run --secret .compost-staging.yaml   # what it would do; stores nothing
compost app deploy --apply --secret .compost-staging.yaml     # store it and deploy, in one step
compost app deploy --apply --prefix staging                   # later: compost.yaml + the stored overlay
compost secret deploy .compost-staging.yaml [--prefix staging]   # store it without deploying
compost secret list
compost secret remove --app myapp --prefix staging
```

The stored overlay must name its app (`name: myapp`). The prefix is `--prefix`, else the file's `prefix`, else `main`. It is kept at `~/.compost-server/secrets/apps/<app>/<prefix>.yaml`.

`app deploy` merges it right after the first file: `compost.yaml` → stored overlay → other `-f` files. Local overlays can still override stored values.

`app deploy --secret <file>` uses the file in place of the stored overlay and stores it with the instance's files, so later deploys need only `compost.yaml`. The file may leave out `name`: the app is the one of the `-f` files, and a different `name` is an error. The prefix is `--prefix`, else the file's, else the other files'. With `--dry-run` nothing is stored. Like `-f` files, it is never uploaded with the sources.

- `secret deploy` and `app deploy --secret` replace the stored overlay as a whole. If the new one leaves out a link that only the old one defined (say an ingress entry with its domains), the next `app deploy` drops that link. Run `app deploy --dry-run` first to see the effect.
- `app remove` keeps the stored overlay, so deploying the instance again restores it as it was. `secret remove` deletes it.
- `app backup` saves it in the archive and `app restore` puts it back; such an archive then holds secrets.

## Local overlays

```sh
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-local.yaml
```

Nothing is stored, so every machine that deploys needs the file. Fine for instances on your machine and throwaway copies.

## Shared apps

Secrets of shared apps go in `.compost-server.secrets.yaml`, next to `compost-server.yaml`, which `server deploy` loads by default:

```yaml
shared:
  database:
    - name: postgres18
      configuration:
        root_password: change-me-to-a-long-random-string
  oidc:
    - name: keycloak
      configuration:
        admin_password: change-me-to-a-long-random-string
  monitoring:
    - name: monitoring
      configuration:
        root_password: Change-me-to-a-long-random-string-1
```

Tokens, webhook URLs and SMTP passwords of [communication apps](Notifications.md#channels) go here too, under `shared.communication`. The credentials of [S3 backup targets](Backup-and-Restore.md#s3-targets) go here too, under `backup.targets.<name>`; backups need them stored on the server (below).

Lists merge by `name`, so only the secret keys are repeated. The passwords are optional. None can change after the first deploy, except an external database's `root_password`, which a new value replaces. Once on the server, they are kept by later deploys without the file. Generated ones are on the server:

```sh
cat ~/.compost-server/shared/database/postgres18/secrets/postgres.env
grep PASSWORD ~/.compost-server/shared/oidc/keycloak/secrets/keycloak.env
grep root_ ~/.compost-server/connectors/monitoring/monitoring/root-connector.yaml
```

### Stored on the server

As with apps, the file can be kept on the server, so any machine deploys with `compost-server.yaml` alone:

```sh
compost server deploy --apply --secret .compost-server.secrets.yaml   # store it and deploy
compost server deploy --apply                                         # later: compost-server.yaml + the stored file
compost secret list
compost secret remove --shared
```

It is kept at `~/.compost-server/secrets/server.yaml` (mode `0600`). `server deploy` merges it right after the first file: `compost-server.yaml` → stored file → other files (`-f`, or `.compost-server.secrets.yaml` when it exists). Local files can still override stored values.

- `--secret` uses the file in place of the stored one and replaces it as a whole. With `--dry-run` nothing is stored. Without `--apply` it is stored with the other files.
- Entries for shared apps that the config doesn't have are left out, with a note: removing a shared app from `compost-server.yaml` doesn't break deploys.
- `server backup` saves it, and `server restore` puts it back when the server has none.

## Notes

- Every instance linked to the same shared app is on that shared app's Docker network. Networks don't isolate instances from each other yet.
- Apps send data to a monitoring app's collector without credentials: any container on its network can. Only the collector holds OpenObserve's password.
- Server backups hold root passwords and link credentials. Keep archives as safe as the server.

---

<!-- Backup-and-Restore.md -->

# Backup and restore

```sh
compost app backup myapp-prod                       # links, sources, volumes → myapp-prod-<time>.compost.tar.gz
compost app backup --all                            # every instance in one archive
compost app backup myapp-prod --link main-db --format raw   # just the SQL dump
compost app restore myapp-prod-….compost.tar.gz --prefix review -f review.yaml   # a copy of the app
compost server backup                               # shared apps: data, config, secrets
compost server restore prod-….compost.tar.gz          # onto a new server, then `app restore`
compost backup run daily                            # a profile: shared apps and every instance, old archives deleted
                                                    # (or by itself, on the server: `schedule` in the profile)
compost backup list                                 # archives on the server
```

Backups take the server's lock, so they never run during a deploy.

## Targets

Where archives go: `--target` for backups, `--source` for restores and `backup list`. Without one, a backup goes to its [profile](#profiles)'s target, else the app's `backup.target` (in `compost.yaml`), else `backup.target` in `compost-server.yaml`, else `local`.

| Target | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `local` | Streamed through the SSH connection to this machine and packed here. Nothing stays on the server. `-o` is a file or folder here. |
| `server` | Packed on the server in its backup folder (`backup.server_path`, default `~/.compost-server/backups`). No data crosses the network. `-o` and restore archives are file names in that folder, or absolute paths. |
| a name from `backup.targets` | A target you define. `type: server` is another folder on the server, e.g. a mounted disk; it works like `server`. `type: s3` is an S3 bucket; see below. |

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
backup:
  target: server
  server_path: backups      # absolute, or relative to compost's folder on the server
  targets:
    nas: {type: server, path: /mnt/nas/compost}
    offsite:
      type: s3
      bucket: acme-backups
      path: prod                                # folder in the bucket (optional)
      endpoint: https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
      region: eu-central-1
```

### S3 targets

An archive for an `s3` target is packed on the server as for `server`, copied to the bucket, then deleted from the server. Restores (`--source offsite`) copy it back into the server's `tmp/` first. `backup list --source offsite` lists the bucket's folder, and `keep` and `backup prune` delete there. The copying is done by [rclone](https://rclone.org) in a container on the server (`rclone/rclone`), so the server needs to reach the bucket; nothing is installed.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `bucket` | required | Bucket name |
| `path` | – | Folder (key prefix) in the bucket |
| `endpoint` | AWS | URL of an S3-compatible service, e.g. Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, Hetzner, MinIO, Garage |
| `region` | – | Region, where the service needs one |
| `provider` | `Other` | rclone's S3 provider, e.g. `AWS`, `Minio`, `Cloudflare`, for provider-specific behavior |
| `access_key_id`, `secret_access_key` | required | Credentials; secrets, see below |
| `image` | `rclone/rclone` of a fixed version | Another rclone image, e.g. from a mirror |

The credentials go in the secrets file, and must be stored on the server, since backups and restores read them there:

```yaml
# .compost-server.secrets.yaml
backup:
  targets:
    offsite: {access_key_id: AKIA…, secret_access_key: …}
```

```sh
compost server deploy --apply --secret .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

They are left out of the stored `compost-server.yaml` and reach rclone in a file readable only by the server user, never on a command line. The key needs to list, read, write and delete objects in that folder; compost doesn't create the bucket.

`app backup --all` without a profile writes one archive, to `--target` or the server's `backup.target`; an app's own `backup.target` applies to backups of that app alone and to profiles.

## Profiles

A profile names a kind of backup: what it saves, where it goes and how many archives of it to keep. Define them in `compost-server.yaml`, where they apply to the shared apps and every app:

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
backup:
  target: server
  profiles:
    daily:     {include: [links], keep: 7, schedule: "0 3 * * *"}   # databases only, every night
    weekly:    {include: [links, sources, volumes], keep: 4, target: nas, schedule: "0 4 * * sun"}
    predeploy: {keep: 3, server: false}                         # apps only; see below
```

```sh
compost backup run daily                         # shared apps and every instance, one archive each
compost app backup myapp-prod --profile weekly   # one instance
compost app backup --all --profile weekly        # every instance, one archive each
compost server backup --profile daily            # the shared apps
compost app backup myapp-prod --profile weekly --target local   # flags override the profile
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `include` | `links,sources,volumes` | Parts of an app backup (as `--include`) |
| `links` | all | Only these links (as `--link`) |
| `format` | `compost` | As `--format` |
| `target` | the app's, then the server's `backup.target` | Where the archives go |
| `keep` | all | Archives kept per instance (and for the shared apps) at the target; older ones are deleted after each backup with the profile |
| `schedule` | – | When the backup runs by itself, as a cron expression; see [Scheduled backups](#scheduled-backups) |
| `server` | `true` | `compost-server.yaml` only: `false` leaves the shared apps out of `backup run` and refuses `server backup --profile` |

An app changes a profile for itself, opts out of it or adds its own in `compost.yaml`. Its profiles also take the app's backup settings, `volumes`, `stop`, `before_backup` and `after_backup`, which replace the app's `backup` keys for that profile:

```yaml
# compost.yaml
backup:
  volumes: [uploads]
  profiles:
    weekly: {keep: 8, schedule: "0 2 * * sat"}   # the other keys come from the server's profile
    daily: false                          # left out of `backup run daily`
    anonymized:                           # this app's own profile
      include: [volumes]
      volumes: [anon-dumps]
      format: raw
      keep: 2
      before_backup:
        - run: anonymizer                 # dumps the database and anonymizes it into anon-dumps; `profiles: [backup]`
                                          # in the compose file keeps `app deploy` from starting it
```

The keys of the app's profile win over the server's, and a key neither sets comes from the app's `backup` settings. Lists replace, they don't add up. The app's profiles take effect with its next `app deploy`, like its other backup settings.

An archive of a profile is named `<instance>-<profile>-<time>`, or `<server>-<profile>-<time>` for the shared apps, and its manifest names the profile. Archives without a profile are never deleted by `keep`.

`backup run` carries on when one instance fails, then exits with an error naming every failure.

### Deleting old archives

`keep` applies after each backup with the profile. To apply it to archives already there, or with another number:

```sh
compost backup prune                       # every profile with `keep`, at each profile's target
compost backup prune --profile daily --keep 3 --target nas --yes
```

It lists what it deletes and asks unless `--yes`. With `--target local` it looks in the current folder.

## Scheduled backups

A profile with a `schedule` runs by itself, on the server, for the shared apps and for every instance it applies to, each on its own:

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
backup:
  profiles:
    daily: {include: [links], keep: 7, schedule: "0 3 * * *"}
```

```sh
compost server deploy --apply      # installs compost on the server and a crontab line
compost server state               # shows each scheduled backup's last run
```

`schedule` is a cron expression in the server's local time: minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, each `*`, a number, a range (`1-5`), a list (`1,15`) or a step (`*/6`). Days of the week are `0`–`7` (Sunday is `0` and `7`) or `mon`…`sun`, months `1`–`12` or `jan`…`dec`. `@hourly`, `@daily`, `@weekly` and `@monthly` work too. When both day of month and day of week are set, either one matches, as in cron.

An app gives a profile its own time with `schedule` in its `compost.yaml`, keeps the profile without a schedule with `schedule: off`, or leaves it with `false`; its own profiles can have a schedule as well:

```yaml
# compost.yaml
backup:
  profiles:
    daily: {schedule: "30 3 * * *"}    # half an hour later than the others
    weekly: {schedule: off}            # only `backup run weekly` or `--profile weekly`
```

**How it runs.** When any profile has a schedule, `server deploy`, `app deploy` and `server restore` put the same version of compost at `~/.compost-server/bin/compost` and add a line to the server user's crontab that runs `compost backup tick` every five minutes. The tick runs every backup whose time has come since its last run, one after another, as `app backup --profile` and `server backup --profile` would: the same archive names, targets and `keep`. It needs nothing from your machine; S3 credentials must be stored on the server (`server deploy --secret`). Its output goes to `~/.compost-server/logs/backup.log`.

- **New schedules** wait for their first time; they don't run at once.
- **Missed times**, e.g. while the server was off, are caught up once at the next tick, if they are less than a month old.
- **Deploys first**: while another command holds the server's lock, the tick waits for it.
- **Results** are kept in `state.yaml`, and a failure (and the next run that works) is [notified](Notifications.md) when `notifications` is set: `server state` lists every scheduled backup with its last run (`ok`, `failed` with the error, or `waiting` for its first run), `app state` those of the instance.
- When no profile has a schedule any more and nothing is notified, the next deploy removes the crontab line; `app remove` does too, if it removed the last scheduled instance.

**Requirements.** The server needs `cron` (the `crontab` command). compost copies itself to the server when it is a static Linux build for the server's CPU (the release builds are) or when the server is this machine; otherwise the server downloads the same release from GitHub and checks it against `SHA256SUMS`, which needs `curl` or `wget`. A development build that can't run on the server can't do either: set `COMPOST_SERVER_BINARY` to a static Linux build to install that one. The line names the server as you defined it (`compost server define`), which goes into the archive names; deploy from machines that use the same name.

**When nothing runs.** If `server state` lists no scheduled backups, or one stays `waiting` past its time, check on the server:

- `crontab -l` has the line between `# compost: scheduled backups of …` and `# compost: end of …`. If not, deploy again (`server deploy --apply`).
- `~/.compost-server/logs/backup.log` grows every five minutes. If it doesn't exist, cron isn't running the line: check that the `cron` service runs, and run the line by hand to see its error.
- `compost backup run <profile>` works. It runs the same backups now, without cron.

## Before a deploy

`deployment.backup` names a profile that `app deploy --apply` runs before it changes an instance that is already deployed:

```yaml
# compost.yaml
deployment:
  backup: predeploy
```

The backup uses the deployed instance's data and links, with the profile as the config being deployed defines it. If it fails, the deploy stops before changing anything. `--backup <profile>` picks another profile for one deploy, `--no-backup` skips it, and `--dry-run` says which one would run. `app restore` and `app rollback` don't take this backup.

## Formats

| `--format` | Writes | Restorable |
|---|---|---|
| `compost` (default) | `<name>.compost.tar.gz` with a manifest and the configuration needed to restore | yes |
| `raw` | Only the data: one item as a plain file (e.g. a `.sql` dump), several as `<name>.tar.gz` | no |

Archives get mode `0600` and never overwrite an existing file. Default names: `<app>-<prefix>-<UTC yyyymmdd-hhmmss>`, `apps-<time>` for `--all`, `<server>-<time>` or `<server>-<shared app>-<time>`.

## App backup

```sh
compost app backup [<instance> | -f files | --app <name> --prefix <prefix> | --all]
                   [--include links,sources,volumes,images] [--link <entry>]… [--stop]
```

| Part | Saved |
|---|---|
| `links` | Database dumps (plain SQL); the objects of storage buckets; ingress, monitoring, key-value and workflow records and site files, for reference. Collected logs and metrics, key-value data and workflows are not part of an app backup |
| `sources` | The uploaded sources (only the compose file when the folder isn't uploaded) |
| `volumes` | The named volumes listed under `backup.volumes` in `compost.yaml` |
| `images` | `docker save` of the services' images |

The default is `links,sources,volumes`. The stored config is always saved, and the overlay stored with `secret deploy`, if any. [Releases](Applications.md#releases-and-rollback) are not saved. `--link main-db` or `--link database:main-db` saves only that link.

Volumes must be listed to be saved:

```yaml
# compost.yaml
backup:
  volumes: [uploads]       # top-level `volumes:` keys of the compose file
```

Links to an [external database](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#external-databases) are dumped too, from a temporary `postgres` client container on the server, with the link's own credentials.

For a consistent copy of files that a service keeps writing, stop it while the volumes are copied. `backup.stop` names those services (`true` for all); `--stop` stops all of them for one backup. They start again afterwards, as do the services that Compose stopped with them; services that weren't running stay stopped.

```yaml
backup:
  volumes: [uploads, search-index]
  stop: [worker, indexer]
```

## Steps around a backup or restore

Some data must be prepared before it is copied, e.g. a database that runs inside the app is dumped into a volume, and loaded from it after a restore. Steps run commands in the instance's services:

```yaml
# compose file
services:
  db:
    image: mariadb:11
    environment: {MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: …}
    volumes: [db-dumps:/dumps, db-data:/var/lib/mysql]
  backup-job:                     # started only by the step: the profile keeps `app deploy` from starting it
    image: myorg/backup-tools
    profiles: [backup]
    volumes: [uploads:/uploads]
volumes: {db-dumps: {}, db-data: {}, uploads: {}}
```

```yaml
# compost.yaml
backup:
  volumes: [db-dumps, uploads]
  before_backup:
    - exec: db
      command: mariadb-dump -uroot -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" --all-databases --single-transaction > /dumps/all.sql
    - run: backup-job             # its own command; or `command: [prepare, --fast]`
  after_backup:
    - {exec: db, command: rm -f /dumps/all.sql}
  after_restore:
    - {exec: db, command: mariadb -uroot -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" < /dumps/all.sql}
```

| Step | Runs | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| `exec: <service>` | `docker compose exec` in the running container; needs `command` | the service isn't running, or the command exits with an error |
| `run: <service>` | `docker compose run --rm`: a new container, removed afterwards; `command` replaces the service's own | the command exits with an error |

A string `command` runs with `sh -c` in the container, so `>`, `<`, `&&` and the container's variables work; a list (`[mariadb, --version]`) runs as is. Steps run on the server in order and their output is shown. They come from the config stored by the last `app deploy`, so deploy after changing them.

| List | When |
|---|---|
| `before_backup` | Before anything of the instance is saved, while its services run. A failed step stops the backup. |
| `after_backup` | After the data is saved and the stopped services started again. Also runs when the backup or a `before_backup` step failed, to clean up; its own failures are warnings. |
| `before_restore` | When data is loaded into a deployed instance (restore without sources): before its services are stopped. A failed step stops the restore. Not run by a restore with sources: that instance only starts after its data is loaded. |
| `after_restore` | After the data is loaded and the services are ready (healthy, for services with a healthcheck), in both kinds of restore. A failed step fails the restore. |

The backup steps run when the backup saves links or volumes (not for `--include sources` or `images` alone).

## App restore

```sh
compost app restore <archive> [--instance <instance> | --all] [--prefix <prefix>] [-f overlays]
                    [--include …] [--link …]… [--replace] [--yes]
```

**With sources** (the default when the archive has them), it deploys the instance from the archive as `app deploy --apply` would, then loads databases, images and volumes before the services start. The archived config is the base; `-f` overlays are merged over it and `--prefix` changes the instance. That makes copies:

```sh
compost app restore myapp-prod-20261015-120000.compost.tar.gz --prefix review -f review-domains.yaml
```

The copy needs other domains (one domain, one instance), and its databases follow the new prefix unless the config sets `db_name`.

**Without sources** (`--include links,volumes`), it loads data into the deployed instance: it lists what will be replaced, asks unless `--yes`, stops the services, loads, and starts them again.

Both run the instance's [restore steps](#steps-around-a-backup-or-restore): those of the restored config with sources, those of the deployed instance without.

Databases and volumes that already hold data are only replaced with `--replace` (exit 3 otherwise). A link's database is created first if it doesn't exist yet, e.g. after `app deploy --no-apply` of a link that moved to another database.

## Moving an app's data to another database

Back up, point the link at the other database, render the deploy without starting it, load the data, deploy:

```sh
compost app backup myapp-prod -o before.compost.tar.gz
# compost.yaml: change `instance` of the database link (e.g. from an external database to compost's)
compost app deploy --no-apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
compost app restore before.compost.tar.gz --include links,volumes --yes
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
```

The old database is left as it was. Volumes move the same way when their name changes, e.g. after removing an `external` volume from a compose override. See [Migration](Migration.md#phase-4-data-into-compost).

## Server backup and restore

```sh
compost server backup [--shared <name>]… [--format …] [-o …] [--target …]
compost server restore <archive> [--shared <name>]… [--source …] [--yes]
```

A server backup holds the stored `compost-server.yaml`, the secrets stored with `server deploy --secret` (restored only when the server has none), all link records and each shared app's data: Postgres `pg_dumpall` and its password file; Caddy's certificates, config and `sites` (for `caddysecurebuild` also its CrowdSec configuration, but not the agent's bans: a restored server starts without bans, with a new bouncer key); OpenObserve's data folder and root login; Temporal's shard count (its workflows are in its Postgres databases). OpenObserve keeps recent data in memory, so it is stopped while its folder is copied (seconds to minutes, depending on its size); the collector keeps retrying what arrives meanwhile for up to five minutes. It holds secrets. External databases are left out; `app backup` saves the apps' data on them.

`server restore` is for a server that doesn't have these shared apps yet (exit 3 if one is deployed). It puts back the records and files, deploys the shared apps, loads their data and then deploys Keycloak and Temporal, which find their data in the restored databases, and OpenObserve, which needs Caddy for its domain. The `monitoring` of shared apps is set up in that last step too.

## Moving to a new server

```sh
compost server backup -o old.compost.tar.gz -s old
compost app backup --all --include sources,volumes,images -o apps.compost.tar.gz -s old

compost server define new --address 198.51.100.7
compost server restore old.compost.tar.gz -s new --yes
compost app restore apps.compost.tar.gz --all -s new --yes
```

The server dump already holds the apps' databases and their link records keep the same credentials, so restore apps without `links`. Point DNS to the new server; Caddy's certificates came along, so there's no wait for Let's Encrypt.

---

<!-- Notifications.md -->

# Notifications

The server tells you when a scheduled backup fails, when a shared app or an instance goes down, and when its disk fills up, and again when each is fine. It sends through **communication apps**: shared apps of the kind `communication`, one per channel. A communication app runs nothing by itself. compost runs its image when it has something to send, with the channel's settings and credentials in a file only the server user can read.

```sh
compost server generate --with matrix    # or webhook, slack, mattermost, discord, email
# add `notifications: {send_to: [ops-matrix]}` to compost-server.yaml
compost server deploy --apply --secret .compost-server.secrets.yaml
compost notify test                      # a test message to every channel
```

## What is sent

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
notifications:
  send_to:
    - ops-chat                                  # every event
    - {to: ops-mail, events: [backup, disk]}    # only these
  disk_free_below: 10                           # percent, default 10
```

| Event | Sent when | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| `backup` | A [scheduled backup](Backup-and-Restore.md#scheduled-backups) failed (with its error), and when that profile's next run works | `error`, then `ok` |
| `health` | A shared app isn't running, or an instance has a container that isn't healthy (as `server state` and `app state` judge it), at two checks in a row; and when it's fine again | `error`, then `ok` |
| `disk` | Free space on the disk with `~/.compost-server` is below `disk_free_below` percent; and when it is 2 points above it again | `warning`, then `ok` |

Each is sent once when it changes, not on every check. The checks run on the server, from the same crontab line as scheduled backups: `server deploy` installs it (and compost itself, see [Scheduled backups](Backup-and-Restore.md#scheduled-backups)) when `send_to` names a channel, and it runs every five minutes. While a deploy holds the server's lock, health isn't checked, so a deploy restarting containers sends nothing. Instances count once deployed with `--apply`. `server state` lists what is currently reported under `alerts (notified)`, and the last state of each check is kept in `state.yaml`.

A channel that can't be reached is logged as a warning in `~/.compost-server/logs/backup.log`, and that message isn't sent again; check channels with `compost notify test`.

## Channels

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
shared:
  communication:
    - name: ops-chat
      type: matrix
      configuration:
        homeserver: https://matrix.example.org
        room: "!abc123:example.org"
    - name: ops-mail
      type: email
      configuration:
        smtp_url: smtps://smtp.example.com:465
        username: alerts@example.com
        from: alerts@example.com
        to: [ops@example.com, oncall@example.com]
```

```yaml
# .compost-server.secrets.yaml
shared:
  communication:
    - name: ops-chat
      configuration: {access_token: syt_…}
    - name: ops-mail
      configuration: {password: …}
```

| Type | Keys | Secret keys |
|---|---|---|
| `webhook` | `url`; `headers` (a map, e.g. `{Authorization: Bearer …}`). Receives JSON: `title`, `severity`, `message`, `server`, `event`, `time` | `url`, `headers` |
| `slack`, `mattermost` | `webhook_url` of an incoming webhook | `webhook_url` |
| `discord` | `webhook_url` of a channel webhook | `webhook_url` |
| `matrix` | `homeserver`; `room`, the room ID under Room settings → Advanced (`!…:server`, or `!` and 43 characters with no server part for rooms of version 12, the default for new rooms on current homeservers); `access_token` of an account that has joined the room | `access_token` |
| `email` | `smtp_url` (`smtps://host:465`, or `smtp://host:587` with STARTTLS); `username`, `password` (optional); `from`; `to` (a list); `require_tls` (default `true`: never send in clear text) | `password` |

Secret keys go in the secrets file. They are left out of the stored `compost-server.yaml` and kept in the app's env file on the server, so later deploys don't need them again; a new value replaces the old one. All values must fit on one line.

Matrix messages are not end-to-end encrypted. In an encrypted room, the homeserver accepts them and Element shows them with a warning.

`server deploy` builds compost's image for communication apps on the server (`compost-communication:<hash>`, from [`images/communication`](https://github.com/devorgpl/compost/tree/master/images/communication): Alpine with `curl` and `jq`), checks that it answers, and shows the app as `on demand` in `server state`. It has no containers, so `server logs` has nothing to show and server backups don't save anything of it.

## Test message

```sh
compost notify test                                  # every communication app
compost notify test --to ops-mail --message "Hello from prod"
```

Each channel says `sent` or why it failed, e.g. `HTTP 403: …` from the service; the command fails if any channel failed.

## Your own image

`image` replaces compost's image with any image that implements the contract, e.g. for a channel compost doesn't have:

```yaml
shared:
  communication:
    - name: ops-pager
      type: webhook                # the type decides the variables compost writes
      image: registry.example.com/pager-notify:2
      configuration: {url: https://pager.example.com/api}
```

compost pulls it on `server deploy` (again with `--pull`) and runs it like its own:

```sh
docker run --rm -i --env-file <file> <image> send --severity <info|warning|error|ok> --title <text> [--server <name>] [--event <id>]  < message
docker run --rm <image> describe
```

- `send` reads the message from stdin (it can have several lines) and exits with `0` once the message is delivered; otherwise with another status and the reason on stderr.
- `describe` prints JSON with at least `"api": 1`; deploys fail without it.
- `--event` is `backup`, `health` or `disk` (none for `notify test`), `--server` the server's name as `compost server define` gave it.
- The env file has `COMMUNICATION_API=1`, `COMMUNICATION_TYPE`, and each configuration key as `COMMUNICATION_<KEY>` in capitals (`to` as a comma-separated list, each header as `COMMUNICATION_HEADER_<n>=Name: value`).
- Keep credentials off command lines inside the container, where the host's `ps` shows them: compost's image passes them to `curl` in a config file.

---

<!-- Configuration.md -->

# Configuration

| File | Where | What |
|---|---|---|
| [`compost.yaml`](#compostyaml) | App repository | How the app is deployed. Commit it. |
| [Overlay](#overlays), e.g. `.compost-staging.yaml` | Anywhere, or stored on the server | Values of one instance, incl. secrets |
| [`compost-server.yaml`](#compost-serveryaml) | Infrastructure folder | The server's shared apps. Commit it. |
| `.compost-server.secrets.yaml` | Infrastructure folder | Shared apps' secrets ([Secrets](Secrets.md#shared-apps)) |
| [`servers.yaml`](#serversyaml), [`config.yaml`](#preferences) | `~/.compost` | Your servers and preferences |

Names (apps, prefixes, shared apps, link entries) use lowercase letters, digits and `-`, start with a letter and have at most 31 characters. App names starting with `compost-` are reserved.

## How files are merged

`-f a.yaml -f b.yaml` or `-f a.yaml,b.yaml` deep-merges the files in order:

1. Maps merge key by key.
2. Lists whose items all have a `name` merge **by name**: matching items merge, new ones are appended.
3. Other lists and values from later files replace earlier ones.

So an overlay only repeats the names and the keys it changes:

```yaml
services:
  ingress:
    - name: site                      # merged into the `site` entry of compost.yaml
      domains: [staging.example.com]
```

Without `-f`: `server deploy` loads `compost-server.yaml` and `.compost-server.secrets.yaml` (if present); `app deploy` loads `compost.yaml`. Overlays stored on the server ([Secrets](Secrets.md)) are merged right after the first file. The merge result plus defaults is the **effective configuration**, which is validated, shown by `--dry-run` and stored on the server without secrets.

## compost.yaml

```yaml
name: myapp                            # required
deployment:
  type: docker-compose                 # the only type
  source_dir: .                        # folder uploaded and holding the compose file; relative to compost.yaml
  compose_file: docker-compose.yaml    # default; relative to source_dir
  compose_overrides: []                # more compose files applied after it; relative to compost.yaml
  build: false                         # false: `pull`; true (or server): `docker compose build` on the server; local (experimental): build on this machine and send the images
  attach_sources: false                # upload the whole folder; forced true by build: true
  releases: 5                          # releases kept on the server for `app rollback`; 0 keeps none
  backup: predeploy                    # backup profile run before `app deploy --apply` changes a deployed instance
services:
  ingress: [ … ]                       # see Applications
  database: [ … ]
  oidc: [ … ]
  monitoring: [ … ]
app_services:
  - name: backend                      # name used by links
    service: backend-webapp            # service in the compose file
    environment:                       # fixed variables
      APP_MODE: production
backup:
  volumes: [uploads]                   # named volumes saved by `app backup`
  stop: [worker]                       # services stopped while volumes are copied; `true` for all
  before_backup: [ … ]                 # steps; see below
  after_backup: [ … ]
  before_restore: [ … ]
  after_restore: [ … ]
  target: nas                          # where this app's backups go
  profiles:                            # changes to the server's profiles, `false` to opt out, or the app's own
    daily: false
    anonymized: {include: [volumes], volumes: [anon-dumps], before_backup: [ … ]}
```

### `backup`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `volumes` | `[]` | Top-level `volumes:` keys of the compose file that `app backup` saves |
| `stop` | none | Compose services stopped while the volumes are copied, or `true` for all; `--stop` stops all |
| `before_backup`, `after_backup` | `[]` | Steps run before anything is saved and after it is saved |
| `before_restore`, `after_restore` | `[]` | Steps run before data is loaded into a deployed instance and after it is loaded |
| `target` | the server's `backup.target` | Target of this app's backups: `local`, `server` or a name from the server's `backup.targets`. A profile's target wins over it |
| `profiles` | `{}` | Per profile: settings that override the server's profile (`include`, `links`, `format`, `target`, `keep`, `schedule` or `schedule: off`, and `volumes`, `stop`, `before_backup`, `after_backup` in place of the keys above), or `false` to opt out. A profile the server doesn't have is the app's own. See [Profiles](Backup-and-Restore.md#profiles) |

Each step is `{exec: <service>, command: …}`, run in the service's running container, or `{run: <service>, command: …}`, a one-off container (`command` optional) that must exit with 0. A string `command` runs with `sh -c`; a list is the command and its arguments. See [Backup and restore](Backup-and-Restore.md#steps-around-a-backup-or-restore).

### `services.ingress[]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | Entry name |
| `domains` | required unless `optional` | Usually in the overlay |
| `optional` | `false` | Skip the entry when no domains are given |
| `routes[].name` | required | |
| `routes[].target` | – | `app_services` name; with `port` |
| `routes[].port` | – | Container port |
| `routes[].path` | `/` | |
| `routes[].strip_prefix` | `false` | Forward `/ui/x` as `/x` |
| `routes[].link` | – | `<kind>/<entry>` of another link instead of `target`/`port`, e.g. `oidc/login` |
| `security.bans` | server default | Block addresses CrowdSec banned. Needs a `caddysecurebuild` ingress, like every `security` key |
| `security.appsec` | server default | Check requests with CrowdSec AppSec |
| `security.rate_limits` | server default | Rate-limit zones of the server, by name; `[]` for none |
| `security.own_rate_limits[]` | `[]` | Zones of this entry: `name`, `paths`, `methods`, `events`, `window` (see [caddysecurebuild](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#caddysecurebuild-ingress)) |

### `services.database[]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | Entry name |
| `type` | required | `postgres`, `mariadb` or `mysql` |
| `version` | `"*"` | Requirement on the major version, e.g. `">=16"` |
| `instance` | – | Pin a shared app by name; required for an external database |
| `targets` | `[]` | `app_services` that get the variables and the network |
| `environment` | `{}` | Variable → `db_host`, `db_port`, `db_name`, `db_user`, `db_password`, `db_url` |
| `db_name`, `db_user` | `<app>_<prefix>_<entry>` | Overlay. `^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]{0,62}$` |
| `db_password` | generated | Overlay, secret. Required for an external database without root credentials |

### `services.keyvalue[]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | Entry name |
| `type` | required | `valkey` or `redis` |
| `version` | `"*"` | Requirement on the major version |
| `instance` | – | Pin a shared app by name |
| `targets` | required | `app_services` that get the variables and the network |
| `environment` | `{}` | Variable → `kv_host`, `kv_port`, `kv_user`, `kv_password`, `kv_db`, `kv_prefix`, `kv_url` |

### `services.storage[]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | Entry name; Garage's bucket is `<app>-<prefix>-<name>` |
| `instance` | – | Pin a storage app by name; required for an external one |
| `targets` | required | `app_services` that get the variables and the network |
| `environment` | `{}` | Variable → `s3_endpoint`, `s3_public_endpoint`, `s3_region`, `s3_bucket`, `s3_access_key_id`, `s3_secret_access_key` |
| `bucket`, `access_key_id`, `secret_access_key` | – | External storage only: the existing bucket and key. Overlay; the keys are secrets |

### `services.oidc[]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name`, `type` | required | `type: keycloak` |
| `version`, `instance` | `"*"`, – | As for databases |
| `realm` | `<app>-<prefix>` | Created if missing |
| `client_id` | `<app>-<prefix>-<entry>` | |
| `public_client` | `false` | No client secret |
| `public_url` | – | The realm's own domain; needs an ingress route with `link: oidc/<entry>` |
| `redirect_uris` | required | |
| `web_origins` | `[]` | |
| `client_secret` | generated | Secret |
| `users[]` | `[]` | `username`, `email`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `password`. Secret |
| `targets`, `environment` | | Values: `oidc_issuer`, `oidc_internal_url`, `oidc_realm`, `oidc_client_id`, `oidc_client_secret` |

### `services.workflow[]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name`, `type` | required | `type: temporal` |
| `version`, `instance` | `"*"`, – | As for databases |
| `namespace` | `<app>-<prefix>` | Created if missing. `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,99}$` |
| `retention_days` | `3` | How long closed workflows are kept |
| `targets` | required | `app_services` that get the variables and the network |
| `environment` | `{}` | Variable → `wf_host`, `wf_port`, `wf_address`, `wf_namespace` |

### `services.monitoring[]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | Entry name |
| `instance` | – | Pin a monitoring app by name; required when the server has several |
| `optional` | `false` | Skip the entry when the server runs no monitoring app |
| `targets` | `[]` | `app_services` whose output is collected and that get the variables and the network |
| `logs` | `true` | Collect the output of `targets`. Fails for a service with its own `logging` |
| `metrics[]` | `[]` | Prometheus endpoints: `target` (`app_services` name), `port`, `path` (default `/metrics`) |
| `environment` | `{}` | Variable → `otlp_endpoint`, `otlp_grpc_endpoint`, `otlp_protocol`, `service_name`, `resource_attributes` |

At least one of `targets` and `metrics` is required.

Details and examples: [Applications](Applications.md).

## Overlays

Same schema as `compost.yaml`, plus `prefix` (default `main`). Typically:

```yaml
prefix: staging
services:
  ingress:
    - name: site
      domains: [staging.example.com]
  database:
    - name: main-db
      db_password: …
app_services:
  - name: backend
    environment:
      APP_MODE: staging
```

An overlay stored with `secret deploy` also needs `name` (`app deploy --secret` adds it). See [Secrets](Secrets.md#overlays-stored-on-the-server).

## compost-server.yaml

```yaml
shared:
  ingress:
    - {name: caddy-main, type: caddy, version: 2, configuration: {…}}
  database:
    - {name: postgres18, type: postgres, version: 18, image: postgres:18-alpine}
    - {name: shop-db, type: postgres, version: 16, external: {host: db, network: shop_default}}
    - {name: mariadb11, type: mariadb, version: 11}
  keyvalue:
    - {name: valkey, type: valkey, version: 9}
  storage:
    - {name: storage, type: garage, configuration: {url: https://files.example.com}}
  oidc:
    - {name: keycloak, type: keycloak, version: 26, configuration: {url: https://auth.example.com}}
  monitoring:
    - {name: monitoring, type: openobserve, version: 1, configuration: {url: https://logs.example.com}}
  workflow:
    - {name: temporal, type: temporal, version: 1, configuration: {ui: {url: https://temporal.example.com, oidc: {}}}}
  communication:
    - {name: ops-chat, type: matrix, configuration: {homeserver: https://matrix.example.org, room: "!abc:example.org"}}
backup:
  target: local                        # local | server | a name from targets
  server_path: backups                 # folder of the server target
  targets:
    nas: {type: server, path: /mnt/nas/compost}   # another folder on the server
    offsite: {type: s3, bucket: acme-backups, path: prod, endpoint: https://s3.example.com}   # credentials in the secrets file
  profiles:
    daily: {include: [links], keep: 7, target: nas, schedule: "0 3 * * *"}
    predeploy: {keep: 3, server: false}
```

```yaml
notifications:
  send_to: [ops-chat, {to: ops-mail, events: [backup, disk]}]   # communication apps; events: backup, health, disk
  disk_free_below: 10                                           # percent
```

See [Notifications](Notifications.md#what-is-sent).

`targets` keys: [S3 targets](Backup-and-Restore.md#s3-targets). `profiles` keys: `include`, `links`, `format`, `target`, `keep`, `schedule` (a cron expression: [Scheduled backups](Backup-and-Restore.md#scheduled-backups)) and `server` (whether `backup run` and the schedule also back up the shared apps, default `true`). See [Profiles](Backup-and-Restore.md#profiles).

Each type's keys: [Servers and shared apps](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#shared-app-types) (communication types: [Notifications](Notifications.md#channels)), and [External databases](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#external-databases) for `external`. At most one ingress per server: `caddy`, or `caddysecurebuild` for Caddy with CrowdSec bans, AppSec and rate limits (its `configuration.security`: [caddysecurebuild](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#caddysecurebuild-ingress)).

Keys every shared app has:

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name`, `type` | required | |
| `version` | per type | Major version |
| `image` | per type | |
| `configuration` | `{}` | The type's keys |
| `external` | – | A server compost doesn't run; databases only |
| `monitoring` | – | Send its output and metrics to a monitoring app: `instance`, `logs` (default `true`), `metrics` (default `true`). See [Monitoring shared apps](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#monitoring-shared-apps) |

## servers.yaml

Written by `server define`; you rarely edit it.

```yaml
servers:
  - name: prod
    connector:
      type: ssh                        # ssh | local
      address: 203.0.113.10
      port: 22                         # optional
      user: compostuser                # default
      identity_file: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # optional; default: ssh config, agent, ~/.ssh/id_*; --ssh-key-file wins
    server_home: ~/.compost-server     # default
    deploy:
      apply: false                     # optional, see below
  - name: dev
    connector:
      type: local
```

## Preferences

```sh
compost config set deploy.apply true [--for-server prod]
compost config unset deploy.apply [--for-server prod]
compost config show
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `deploy.apply` | `false` | `server deploy` and `app deploy` start services without `--apply` |

`--apply`/`--no-apply` win over the server's value, which wins over the global one in `~/.compost/config.yaml`.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `COMPOST_HOME` | compost's local folder, default `~/.compost` |
| `COMPOST_SERVER` | Target server, when `-s` isn't given (wins over the context) |
| `COMPOST_SSH_KEY_FILE` | SSH private key, when `--ssh-key-file` isn't given (wins over the server's `identity_file`) |
| `COMPOST_SERVER_BINARY` | compost binary that deploys install on the server for [scheduled backups](Backup-and-Restore.md#scheduled-backups), instead of this one or a download |
